Interesting read, but the skeptic in me picked up on:

The only other problem the test now has is that it needs to be properly developed and brought to market.

That is a pretty bold claim. I think the the journalist could have been more rigorous by stating:

The only other known problem the test now has is that it needs to be properly developed and brought to market.

Seemingly small distinction, but removes the claimed universal statement.

Problem is this: You don't know for certain that a specific antibody = a particular virus. And you don't know all the viruses that are out there or which one's not yet known are causing some harm.

Every antibody we generate is a random product screened as being non-self from a slew of other "hypervariable" products.. We are talking many billions of random combinations. We don't actually tailor or create new antibody "blue prints" in response to exposure to a new epitope. Antibodies are more like the body throwing pasta at the wall and seeing what sticks.

If the epitope is sufficiently different from our own self epitopes then the antibody will "stick" and the process of ramping up production of that specific antibody(s) is undertaken.

These antibodies may or may not even be effective (or necessary) in fighting or killing an invading virus and it may even be a mistake and spark a autoimmune process. The epitope of the antigen is not exclusive, either. Many different antigens might just share the same epitope.

So basing a test for definitive past virus identity based purely on IgG antibodies still circulating in the blood is a leap. False negatives and false positives will abound for known viruses. And unknown viruses that are actually causing pathology?

Forget about it. Just eat the bluegreen algae-virus and stop thinking so hard.

PCR for the actual DNA or RNA of the virus gets us much closer to certainty and even can clue us in to the magnitude of the viral infection.

So I'm going to put this is in flowchart style. Assume we're browsing /v/all. This assumes the user is taking a positive approach (as in, I will voat).

[START] Is this an obvious troll post?

For example, from a time to time a user will decide they should spam /v/askvoat with a series of loaded questions that disregard their incendiary nature. While this user may be legit in their own right, they clearly have some agenda (even if it's just to get a rise out of you). This content is legal in the target sub, but while the first post in the series mighte have been interesting, the 8th is just obnoxious.

THAT WAS JUST AN EXAMPLE, ADAPT ACCORDINGLY.

IF Yes: DOWNVOAT

ELSE:

[1] Do you care about the subject matter?

IF Yes:

Check the link/read the post. Does it meets your minimum standards for "should not be nuked"?

IF Yes: UPVOAT

ELSE:

[2] Does this post break any particular rules of the sub?

IF Yes: DOWNVOAT

IF No, but it should: REPORT TO MOD. Tell them specifically why you think the rules suck.

ELSE:

Do you think other people interested in the subject matter might be interested in this?

IF Yes: UPVOAT or IGNORE

Hope this helps. :)
